pangolin.title: Walking Pinecones
pangolin.fact: Pangolins are the only mammals covered in scales! When threatened, they roll into a tight ball, making them look like living pinecones.

pangolin.title: Armored Squirrels
pangolin.fact: Pangolins are the only mammals covered in scales, making them look like real-life armadillos! When threatened, they can curl up into a tight ball, using these scales as armor against predators.

pangolin.title: A Tongue Longer Than Its Body
pangolin.fact: Pangolins have no teeth at all. Instead they rely on a sticky tongue that can stretch longer than their own head and body combined, anchored all the way back near their pelvis, to slurp up ants and termites by the thousands.

pangolin.title: The Stomach That Chews
pangolin.fact: Pangolins have no teeth, so the stomach does the chewing instead. Its far end is thick and muscular, lined with hard keratin spines pointing inward, and it usually holds small stones the pangolin has swallowed. Together they grind whole insects apart much the way a bird's gizzard does.

pangolin.title: 70 Million Insects a Year
pangolin.fact: One adult pangolin can eat more than 70 million insects in a single year, almost all of them ants and termites. All that digging turns over organic matter and aerates the soil, and the burrows they abandon get taken over by other animals looking for shelter.

pangolin.title: Armor Written Into the Genome
pangolin.fact: When researchers sequenced pangolin genomes in 2016, they found broken copies of tooth-building genes still sitting in the DNA but no longer read. They also found that a gene tied to the skin's ability to fight disease has stopped working, which hints that pangolins came to lean on their scales for protection instead.

pangolin.title: Scales With a Return Address
pangolin.fact: Asian and African pangolins have been on separate evolutionary paths for at least 23 million years. A Smithsonian-led team used that deep split to build a genetic family tree covering all eight species, giving investigators markers that can trace a seized scale back to the species it came from.

pangolin.title: Fingernails, Basically
pangolin.fact: Pangolin scales are keratin, the same protein your fingernails and hair are made of. That has done nothing to slow demand: when the IUCN reviewed seizures logged between 2016 and 2024, scales made up 99 percent of every confiscated pangolin part.

fennec-fox.title: Ears That Work as Radiators
fennec-fox.fact: A fennec's ears run to about 15 centimetres on an animal that weighs under two kilograms, the largest ears relative to body size of any carnivore. They are not only for listening. They carry a dense network of shallow blood vessels, and the fox dumps heat through them into the air, which lets it hold its temperature down without panting away water it cannot spare. The hearing is real too: a fennec can track insects and small rodents moving under the sand and dig straight down onto them.

fennec-fox.title: It Can Live Without Drinking
fennec-fox.fact: A fennec can go its whole life without drinking free water. It takes moisture from what it eats, and its kidneys concentrate urine far enough to keep the loss on the other side very small. Burrowing does the rest, since the air down in the den stays cooler and far more humid than the surface. Given water a fennec will drink it, but in most of its range there is nothing to drink.

fennec-fox.title: Fur on the Soles of Its Feet
fennec-fox.fact: The undersides of a fennec's feet are covered in thick fur, right over the pads. It works as insulation on sand hot enough to burn an unprotected foot, and it spreads the animal's weight so it can move across a loose surface without sinking. The same feet dig fast. A fennec can put itself out of sight underground in a few seconds, and dens often run several metres with more than one way out.

capybara.title: The Chillest Animal
capybara.fact: Capybaras are so relaxed they often let other animals sit on them: birds, monkeys, even caimans! They're the largest rodents in the world and native to South America.

capybara.title: Built-In Snorkel Mode
capybara.fact: Capybaras can hold their breath underwater for up to 5 minutes to hide from jaguars and caimans. Their eyes, ears, and nostrils sit high on their head, like a hippo's, so they can stay almost fully submerged and still see, hear, and breathe.

narwhal.title: Unicorn of the Sea
narwhal.fact: Narwhals have a long spiral tusk (up to 10 feet!) that is actually a tooth. Scientists believe they use it to sense water temperature and salinity.

narwhal.title: Super Sneaky Narwhal
narwhal.fact: Narwhals are often called the unicorns of the sea, thanks to their long, spiral tusks that can grow up to 10 feet long! Surprisingly, this tusk is actually an elongated tooth, and scientists believe it can detect changes in the environment, helping these mystical creatures navigate the frigid Arctic waters.

aye-aye.title: The Finger That Finds Grubs
aye-aye.fact: An aye-aye's middle finger is thin, skeletal, and double-jointed, built to tap on tree bark up to eight times a second and listen for hollow spots where grubs are hiding. Once it finds one, that same finger reaches in and hooks the grub out, a foraging trick found nowhere else in the animal kingdom.

thorny-devil.title: Drinks Through Its Skin
thorny-devil.fact: Thorny devils never need to drink with their mouths. Grooves between their spiky scales pull water in by capillary action from any damp surface, including morning dew, channeling it straight to their mouth. When threatened, they also tuck their real head down and present a fake spiked 'head' on the back of their neck instead.

panther-chameleon.title: Color Means Communication
panther-chameleon.fact: Chameleons don't change color primarily for camouflage. They do it to communicate mood and temperature. Color changes signal stress, excitement, readiness to mate, and more.

panther-chameleon.title: Color-Changing Camouflage
panther-chameleon.fact: Chameleons are famous for their ability to change color, but did you know it's primarily a way to communicate? They alter their hues depending on their mood and social signals, rather than just blending into their surroundings!

panther-chameleon.title: Chameleon Color Change
panther-chameleon.fact: Chameleons are famous for their color-changing abilities, but it's not just for camouflage! They change colors in response to mood, temperature, and even social signals, making them masters of both disguise and emotion!

panther-chameleon.title: Faster Than a Fighter Pilot
panther-chameleon.fact: A chameleon's tongue accelerates fast enough to briefly pull more G-force than a human fighter pilot can withstand. It can strike a full body-length away and snap back with its prey in a fraction of a second.

green-anaconda.title: Heaviest, Not Longest
green-anaconda.fact: The green anaconda is the heaviest snake alive and routinely gets called the biggest, which is only half right. Reticulated pythons grow longer, past seven metres, but an anaconda is built on a completely different scale of thickness and can pass 100 kilograms where a python of similar length is nowhere near it. Reliable measurements are rarer than the stories suggest. Claims above nine metres have circulated for over a century without one being confirmed.

green-anaconda.title: Constriction Is About Blood, Not Bones
green-anaconda.fact: The old description of constriction is that the snake crushes its prey or suffocates it. Measurements on constricting snakes point somewhere else: the pressure a large constrictor applies is enough to stop blood circulating, and circulatory arrest kills far faster than suffocation would. The snake tightens as its prey breathes out, so each exhalation gives away a little more room and never gets it back.

green-anaconda.title: It Gives Birth, It Does Not Lay Eggs
green-anaconda.fact: Anacondas are viviparous. Females carry their young internally and give birth to live snakes, often twenty to forty at a time, each already around half a metre long and able to swim and hunt immediately. There is no parental care after that. Females are also far larger than males, which is unusual enough among snakes to be worth saying plainly: a big female can be several times the weight of any male she breeds with.

glass-frog.title: See-Through Bellies
glass-frog.fact: Some glass frogs have skin on their underside so transparent you can watch their heart beating and blood moving through their organs. While they sleep, they pack nearly all their red blood cells into their liver, making themselves even harder for predators to spot against a leaf.

blue-poison-dart-frog.title: It Is Not a Separate Species
blue-poison-dart-frog.fact: The blue poison dart frog is one of the most photographed frogs on Earth and it is not its own species. It is a color morph of Dendrobates tinctorius, a widespread South American frog whose populations look startlingly different from one patch of forest to the next. The blue form comes from isolated forest islands in southern Suriname, cut off in savannah, and the name azureus it was given as a species is now treated as one of those local forms rather than a species boundary.

blue-poison-dart-frog.title: Captive Ones Are Harmless
blue-poison-dart-frog.fact: These frogs do not make their toxins. They accumulate them from what they eat in the wild, mainly mites and ants carrying alkaloids of their own, and concentrate the compounds in glands in the skin. Take that diet away and the toxicity goes with it. Captive-bred frogs raised on fruit flies and springtails are effectively non-toxic, which is why keeping one is possible at all and why a wild-caught animal is a completely different proposition.

blue-poison-dart-frog.title: The Poison Dart Name Is Borrowed
blue-poison-dart-frog.fact: Around 170 species get called poison dart frogs and only three were ever used that way, all in the genus Phyllobates, in a small area of western Colombia. Hunters wiped a dart tip across a frog's back and the coating stayed effective for months. Every other species picked the name up by association, this one included, and no hunter has ever tipped a dart with it.

axolotl.title: Axolotl Superpowers
axolotl.fact: Axolotls can regenerate entire limbs, their heart, spinal cord, and even parts of their brain with zero scarring! Scientists study them hoping to unlock regeneration secrets for humans.

axolotl.title: Forever Young, Forever Underwater
axolotl.fact: Axolotls never grow up in the usual salamander sense. Thanks to a trait called neoteny, they keep their feathery gills and stay fully aquatic for their entire lives, reaching adulthood without ever setting foot on land. Sadly, the wild population now survives in just one place, a shrinking canal system near Mexico City.

shoebill.title: The Statue That Hunts
shoebill.fact: Shoebills can stand completely motionless for hours while hunting, then explode into a violent strike so fast it can snap a lungfish or baby crocodile in half. Their clog-shaped bill has sharp edges specifically for slicing through tough prey.

victoria-crowned-pigeon.title: A Pigeon the Size of a Turkey
victoria-crowned-pigeon.fact: The Victoria crowned pigeon is the largest pigeon in the world, around 75 centimetres long and up to roughly 2.5 kilograms, which is to say a pigeon you would notice from across a field. It is blue-grey with a maroon breast, a deep red eye, and a fan of crest feathers standing upright on its head. It spends nearly all of its time walking the forest floor of northern New Guinea, and flies up mainly to roost or to get away from something.

victoria-crowned-pigeon.title: The Crest Is Lace, Not Spikes
victoria-crowned-pigeon.fact: Up close the crown is not the stiff fan it looks like at a distance. Each feather in it has a bare shaft for most of its length and opens into a small triangular tip of white barbs at the end, so the whole crest reads as an open mesh with a dotted white edge. Two other crowned pigeon species carry their own versions, and the white tips are the quickest way to tell this one apart from them.

victoria-crowned-pigeon.title: Both Parents Make Milk
victoria-crowned-pigeon.fact: Pigeons feed their chicks on crop milk, a thick protein and fat rich secretion produced by cells lining the crop, and both the male and the female make it. It is not milk in any mammalian sense and contains no lactose, but it does the same job, and a crowned pigeon chick lives on nothing else for its first days. Pairs usually raise a single chick, and both birds sit the egg, the male through the day and the female overnight.

manta-ray.title: Ocean's Biggest Brain
manta-ray.fact: Giant manta rays have the largest brain relative to body size of any fish, rivaling the ratios seen in some mammals. In mirror tests, they spend far more time in front of a real mirror than a blank panel and repeatedly perform unusual movements like blowing bubbles while watching themselves, behavior researchers think hints at some level of self-awareness.

leafy-sea-dragon.title: Leaves That Learned to Swim
leafy-sea-dragon.fact: Leafy sea dragons are covered in leaf-shaped skin flaps that serve purely as camouflage. They actually swim using nearly invisible fins on their neck and back, so from a distance they look like drifting seaweed rather than a fish at all.
